summary: Defines a MIB module for managing MAC bridges based on IEEE 802.1D-1998 between LAN segments. It supports transparent bridging and covers other bridging types. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: This document defines the SNMP objects that describe a network bridge: a device that connects LAN segments below the network layer by forwarding frames. It covers the bridge's ports, its spanning tree, the forwarding table of addresses it has learned, and any static filters set on it.

questions: how to monitor spanning tree with snmp
subtitle: The SNMP object definitions that let a manager read and configure an Ethernet-style bridge and its spanning tree.

tldr.problem: A manager needs to see what a bridge is doing: how many ports it has, what the spanning tree looks like, which MAC addresses it has learned and where, and which static filters are configured.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the BRIDGE-MIB as a translation of the earlier RFC 1493 module into SMIv2 syntax, with objects arranged into subtrees for the bridge base, the spanning tree, source routing, transparent bridging and static filtering.
tldr.outcome: The module covers transparent bridging, as defined in IEEE 802.1D, and leaves objects out where another MIB already provides the same information. It obsoletes RFC 1493.

facts.label: Static filter port set
facts.value: One bit per port, in an octet string of up to 512 octets

today: RFC 4188 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2005. It obsoleted RFC 1493 and has not been obsoleted since. It is the SMIv2 translation of the bridge management objects defined in IEEE 802.1D.

sections.title: What the Bridge MIB Covers
sections.content:
A common device present in many networks is the bridge, used to connect Local Area Network segments below the network layer. There are two major modes defined for this bridging: transparent and source route. The transparent method of bridging is defined in the IEEE 802.1D specification, and this memo defines the objects needed for the management of a bridging entity that operates in transparent mode, as well as some objects that apply to all types of bridges. Provisions are also made so that these objects apply to bridges connected by subnetworks other than LAN segments.

The MIB module presented in the memo is a translation of the BRIDGE-MIB defined in RFC 1493 into SMIv2 syntax, and it obsoletes that earlier document.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB describes a bridge in the way a management system needs: what it is attached to, how it forwards frames, and what its spanning tree looks like. It is the same set of objects as the older RFC, rewritten in the newer management definition language.

sections.title: Design Goals and the Objects Left Out
sections.content:
To be consistent with IAB directives and good engineering practice, an explicit attempt was made to keep the module as simple as possible. Six criteria were applied to the objects proposed for inclusion: start with a small set of essential objects and add only as further objects are needed; require that objects be essential for either fault or configuration management; consider evidence of current use or utility; limit the total number of objects; exclude objects that are simply derivable from others in this or other MIB modules; and avoid causing critical sections to be heavily instrumented, with the guideline followed being one counter per critical section per layer.

The same reasoning explains what was left out. Bridge.BridgeName is the same as sysDescr in the SNMPv2-MIB, Bridge.BridgeUpTime is the same as sysUpTime, Bridge.PortAddresses is the same as ifPhysAddress in the IF-MIB, and BridgePort.PortName and BridgePort.PortType are the same as ifDescr and ifType. BridgePort.RoutingType is derivable from the subtrees that are implemented. The SpanningTreeProtocol.BridgeIdentifier is a combination of dot1dStpPriority and dot1dBaseBridgeAddress, and SpanningTreeProtocolPort.PortIdentifier is a combination of dot1dStpPort and dot1dStpPortPriority. The TopologyChange and TopologyChangeAcknowledged objects were left out because they are transitory, and DiscardLackOfBuffers is redundant. The Transmission Priority objects are not required by the Pics Proforma and are not considered useful.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors kept the module small on purpose. Anything another MIB already provides, anything that can be worked out from other objects, and anything that changes only briefly is left out, so the module does not grow without need.

sections.title: The Five Subtrees
sections.content:
Objects in the module are arranged into subtrees, each a set of related objects, and the module itself sits at the object identifier mib-2 17 as dot1dBridge.

The dot1dBase subtree contains the objects applicable to all types of bridges: the bridge address, the number of ports, the type of bridging the entity can perform, with values unknown, transparent-only, sourceroute-only and srt, and a generic port table holding information about every port associated with the bridge, including transparent, source-route and srt ports. Each port row carries the port number, the ifIndex of the interface behind it, the circuit, and the discards caused by delay exceeded and by the MTU being exceeded.

The dot1dStp subtree holds the bridge's state with respect to the Spanning Tree Protocol. If a node does not implement the Spanning Tree Protocol, this subtree will not be implemented. It carries the protocol specification and bridge priority, the time since the last topology change and the number of topology changes, the designated root, root cost and root port, the MaxAge, HelloTime and HoldTime values, the ForwardDelay and the bridge's own MaxAge, HelloTime and ForwardDelay, and a port table with per-port priority, state, enable, path cost, designated root, designated cost, designated bridge, designated port and forward transitions.

The dot1dSr subtree describes the entity's state with respect to source route bridging, as described in RFC 1525, and applies only to that kind of bridge. The dot1dTp subtree describes the entity's state with respect to transparent bridging; if transparent bridging is not supported it will not be implemented, and it applies to transparent-only and SRT bridges. The dot1dStatic subtree describes the entity's state with respect to destination-address filtering, applies to any type of bridge that performs it, and will not be implemented if that filtering is not supported.
sections.plainLanguage: The objects are grouped into five sets: what every bridge has, what the spanning tree is doing, what source routing is doing, what transparent forwarding is doing, and what static filters are configured. A bridge only implements the sets that apply to it.

sections.title: Ports, Interfaces and Other MIB Modules
sections.content:
Full support for the 802.1D management objects requires that the SNMPv2-MIB objects sysDescr and sysUpTime be implemented, and that the IF-MIB objects ifIndex, ifType, ifDescr, ifPhysAddress and ifLastChange be implemented. The SNMPv2-MIB objects apply to the device as a whole, whether bridging is the device's only function or only part of it.

Implicit in the BRIDGE-MIB is the notion of ports on a bridge. Each port is associated with one interface of the interfaces subtree, and in most situations each port is associated with a different interface, but there are situations in which several ports share one interface, for example several ports corresponding one-to-one with several X.25 virtual circuits that are all on the same interface. Each port is uniquely identified by a port number, which has no mandatory relationship to an interface number, although in the simple case the port number has the same value as the corresponding interface's number. Port numbers are in the range 1 to dot1dBaseNumPorts.

The IF-MIB treats a network interface as being attached to a 'subnetwork', which is not to be confused with 'subnet', an addressing partitioning scheme used in the Internet suite of protocols. The memo uses the term 'segment' for such a subnetwork, whether it is an Ethernet segment, a 'ring', a WAN link, or even an X.25 virtual circuit.

Some entities perform other functions as well as bridging. Where an entity routes IP datagrams and only bridges other protocols, only the non-IP data is considered to have been bridged. The BRIDGE-MIB, and in particular its counters, therefore apply only to the subset of the data on an entity's interfaces that is sent or received for a protocol being bridged, and all such data travels through the ports of the bridge.
sections.plainLanguage: A port is not the same thing as an interface, although usually one port sits on one interface. The counters only count the traffic the bridge actually forwards, not everything the device handles, and a 'segment' here means whatever kind of link the port is attached to.

sections.title: The Forwarding Database and Static Filters
sections.content:
The dot1dTp subtree holds the transparent bridging state. dot1dTpLearnedEntryDiscards counts the entries the bridge had to discard because its forwarding database was full, and dot1dTpAgingTime is how long a learned entry is kept before it ages out. The dot1dTpFdbTable is the forwarding database itself, one row per MAC address the bridge has an entry for, with the address, the port the address was learned on, and a status: other, meaning that some other object is determining how frames to that address are forwarded; invalid, meaning the entry is no longer valid, for example because it aged out, but has not yet been flushed; learned, meaning the port was learned and is in use; self, meaning the address is one of the bridge's own and the port says which of its ports has it; and mgmt, meaning the address also appears in the static table.

The dot1dTpPortTable holds per-port counters for transparent bridging, with a MaxInfo field and counts of frames received, frames forwarded and frames discarded inbound. The dot1dStaticTable holds filtering configured by management, specifying the set of ports to which frames received from specific ports and containing specific destination addresses are allowed to be forwarded. The value zero in that table, as the port number from which frames with a specific destination address are received, means all ports for which there is no specific entry for that destination address. Entries are valid for unicast and for group and broadcast addresses.

Each static entry names a destination MAC address, the receive port, and the set of ports the frames may go to. That set is held in an octet string where each octet covers eight ports, the first octet covering ports 1 to 8, and within each octet the most significant bit represents the lowest numbered port. The default is a string of ones of the appropriate length.
sections.plainLanguage: The forwarding table lists the addresses the bridge has learned and which port each one is on. The static table is a filter: for a given source port and destination address, it says which ports frames are allowed to go out on.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A number of management objects defined in this module have a MAX-ACCESS clause of read-write or read-create, and such objects may be considered sensitive or vulnerable in some network environments. The support for SET operations in a non-secure environment without proper protection can have a negative effect on network operations. Some of the readable objects may also be considered sensitive, so it is important to control even GET and NOTIFY access to them and possibly to encrypt their values when sending them over the network via SNMP.

The RFC then works through which objects matter. The writable objects dot1dStpPriority, dot1dStpBridgeMaxAge, dot1dStpBridgeHelloTime, dot1dStpBridgeForwardDelay, dot1dStpPortPriority, dot1dStpPortEnable, dot1dStpPortPathCost and dot1dStpPortPathCost32 influence the spanning tree protocol, so unauthorized write access can make the protocol compute other default topologies or change how quickly it reacts to failures. The writable object dot1dTpAgingTime controls how fast dynamically learned forwarding information ages out, and setting it to a large value may simplify forwarding table overflow attacks. The writable dot1dStaticTable provides the filtering mechanism that controls to which ports frames from a specific source may be forwarded, so write access can be used to turn provisioned filtering off or to add filters that prevent rightful use of the network.

The readable objects provide information about the topology of a bridged network and the attached active stations. The addresses listed in the dot1dTpFdbTable usually reveal the manufacturer of the MAC hardware, which can be useful for mounting other specific attacks. The two notifications newRoot and topologyChange are emitted during spanning tree computation and may trigger management systems to inspect the status of bridges and recompute internal topology information, so forged notifications may make management systems perform unnecessary computations and generate additional SNMP traffic, and may therefore be part of a denial of service attack.

SNMP versions prior to SNMPv3 did not include adequate security, and even on a secure network there is no control over who may GET or SET the objects in this module. The RFC recommends the security features of the SNMPv3 framework, including full support for its cryptographic mechanisms, and that deployment of earlier SNMP versions is NOT RECOMMENDED, leaving it to the operator to configure access so that only principals with legitimate rights can read or change the objects.
sections.plainLanguage: Writing the spanning tree objects can change the shape of the network or slow the tree's reaction to a failure, and writing the filters can lock other stations out. Reading the forwarding table reveals which hardware is on the network. The RFC therefore recommends SNMPv3 with authentication and privacy.

sections.title: Changes From RFC 1493
sections.content: The MIB definitions were translated to use SMIv2, which includes the introduction of conformance statements. ASN.1 type definitions were converted into textual conventions, and several UNITS clauses were added. The object dot1dStpPortPathCost32 was added to support IEEE 802.1t, and the permissible values for dot1dStpPriority and dot1dStpPortPriority were clarified for bridges supporting IEEE 802.1t or IEEE 802.1w. The interpretation of dot1dStpTimeSinceTopologyChange was clarified for bridges supporting the rapid spanning tree protocol. The introductory boilerplate, the security considerations section and the references were updated to comply with current IETF standards and guidelines, references were updated to point to newer IEEE 802.1d documents, and additions and clarifications were made in various description clauses.
sections.plainLanguage: The objects themselves are much the same as in the earlier RFC. The main work was rewriting them in the current management definition language, adding one path cost object for faster spanning tree, and tightening the wording.
